content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:105
- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size, and read as values in a coercion's body they are exact integers, `ZZ`; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Rows 969 and 970 hold the tree's run-time numeral with its four numbers as fields.

POSITIONS.md:106
- P-176 **A numeral at a place denotes one value, the same on both paths and made once: the compiler folds the coercion instantiated for it (P-174), and walk runs that coercion at the place's first evaluation.** Where the result is a JVM `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, the class file holds it as a constant; otherwise, as at `QQ` or a program's own type, the constructor call on the constants runs once per place, into a `static final` field filled when the class loads, and a program's type's own `-` on the numeral (P-174) runs there too. Walk fixes the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers and keeps the result for the place; it refuses a numeral only when the place runs, until it runs the checker (P-12). Before the switch-over the compiler's prelude carries this design (P-37), so that both paths give one value at one place. Why: a numeral is a constant of the program, and a JVM class file holds no object, so a field filled once at load is the nearest form of an object constant. Rows 969 and 970 hold where the tree departs.

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The one exception is the numerals: until the switch-over the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176, so that both paths treat a numeral alike before it, and that copy goes with the prelude. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

POSITIONS.md:38
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). The bound is this implementation's, for the sizes of arrays, vectors and matrices, to match the JVM's `int` indices; a numeral type's four static parameters have none, and read as values are `ZZ` (P-174). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:99
- P-165 **`asFloat` and the `=` built on it leave `trait Number`; each built-in number type keeps its own `asFloat`.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` each declare `asFloat`, so the written conversion `asFloat(x)` into `RR64` is unchanged at every concrete type; the numeral types declare none, since no numeral value exists when a program runs (P-174). Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other (P-74); otherwise the program writes the conversion, `asFloat(x) = y`. The vector norm takes a bound that promises a float; its form is the default of a fork on his review list: the norm at each of the eight number types, each by its own `asFloat` (F-324). `Float`'s `^` at a `Number` exponent, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo` are declared at `RR64`, and coercion carries `ZZ32`, `RR32` and numerals to them. The specification's sentence follows (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:56-73`). P-74's rule, an exact conversion implicit and a lossy one written, stands. Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:510`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision. The curator's rule for such a case: an early idea of the interpreter's library goes where the specification does not ground it and the later prelude eliminated it. With `Number` open (P-160), an abstract `asFloat` would force a program's own number, such as a complex number, to invent a float, and `Number`'s `=` would compare two different complex numbers by it.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:62
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:89
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.

== explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md:33-63

## 3. The design, as reflected back to him and confirmed

Confirmed on 11-09: "Yes, I see no wrong sentence."

1. **A numeral has a type at compile time only:** `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with the four numbers as static parameters. `3.125` has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. The parser gives the compiler the four numbers; the checker carries them in the type. These types live in the checker. When the program runs there is no numeral object, no method on one, nothing of the numeral left. `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are gone.

2. **Where a type is fixed, the compiler converts the numeral at compile time, from the exact value.** Constant folding. Into an integer type exactly, or a refusal at compile time when it does not fit. Into `QQ` exactly. Into `RR64` or `RR32` with one rounding. The class file holds the finished constant. Walk gives the same value at the same place.

3. **A program's own number type gets numerals by declaring a coercion whose parameter is the numeral type, generic over the four numbers.** The Draft's interval, as the coordinator showed him at 21:35 (L4685):

   ```
   object Interval(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
     coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =
       Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))
   end
   iv: Interval = 3.1415926535897932384
   ```

   The coercion is not a method that runs on a value. It is the interface the type implements so that the compiler can hand it the four numbers from the source. Its body is a call of the type's constructor with values computed from `n, m, r, v`. The compiler knows the four numbers, so it instantiates the coercion for that numeral and emits the constructor call with the constants. The result is a constant of the program: one object per site, computed once. No double in between. The one JVM detail he accepted at 22:21: a class file cannot hold an object as a constant, so that object is built once when the class loads, into a `static final` field, and every use reads it.

4. **`nat` is a natural number with no bound in the type system.** The 32-bit `nat` is this implementation's choice for the JVM's array sizes, not the language's. So `v` of a 20-digit numeral in a static parameter is fine in the design; the checker must hold it.

5. **Where nothing fixes a type**, `x = 3`, `f(3)` at `Any`, `Cell(3)`: the machine default, `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by size, and `RR64`. Then point 2 applies: converted at compile time into the default. His decision of 22:40.

6. **An expression of numerals alone folds first, exactly:** `3 + 4`, `1/2`, `-3`, `6.0221415 × 10^23`. Then the folded constant converts or defaults like a numeral. A numeral has no sign; `-3` is the minus applied to `3` (his 23:10; the judgement's repair 3).

7. **Both paths do the same thing, before the switch-over.** A user sees no difference between walk and the compiled path.

8. **The proof is his own types, run on both paths:** complex from `3 + 4 i`; the Draft's interval; `Dec(unscaled, scale)` receiving `3.14159` as 314159 and 5; bfloat16 rounding once from the exact value; the round trip, the type's own method printing `C.8_16` back from the four constants; a compile-time range check, a byte type that refuses `300` before the program runs, the one thing static parameters give that run-time fields cannot; `0.1_2 SEQV 0.5` true, `0.1 = 0.1_16` false.

**His addition on 11-09, after the confirmation.** The library's own number types (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32`, `RR64`) take numerals by the same mechanism as a program's types: a coercion from the numeral type, generic over the four numbers, folded by the compiler. No separate way in the compiler for the shipped numerics, and no excuses for them. An efficient implementation through the same mechanism is a stress test of the design: if the library's types come out fast through the common mechanism, the mechanism is right. This matches the Draft's "Libraries define coercions from numerals to integers ... and rational numbers."

== explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md:65-70

## 4. What it is not

- Not a `Numeral` value object with getters for the four numbers, `asFloat`, `asString` and `=` pairs with the number types.
- Not a coercion called at run time on such an object.
- Not the compiler prelude's `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral`.
- Not walk building a numeral object at a site's first evaluation and calling the coercion on it.

== explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md:143-156

## 11. Consequences talked through on 2026-11-09, 15:xx to 16:3x UTC

He confirmed each as a consequence of the design, not a choice ("There is no alternative here").

- The library's own number types take numerals by the same generic coercion as a program's type (the Draft: "Libraries define coercions from numerals to integers ... and rational numbers"). The compiler's folding for a built-in type is the folding of a constructor call whose result is a JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. A separate way in the compiler for the shipped numerics is a hole in the design.
- `-3` at a program's own type: the coercion receives the written numeral `3`; the type's own `opr -(self)` (the additive group's operation, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:267-271`) applies to the result; both run once, when the class loads, so the whole `-3` at that place is one constant. A type without `-` refuses `-3`. Batch 29's fold, which hands the coercion a signed value (rows 961, 968, queue item 448), is wrong; the revised specification's sentence (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:215-218`) is right.
- `-2147483648` at `ZZ32`: the static expression folds exactly first, then converts (his 23:10 to 23:23 on 11-08, repair 3).
- `2 + 3` or `1/2` at a program's own type: by repair 3's "a written numeral only", only a written numeral goes through the numeral coercion; `2 + 3` is two `ZZ32` defaults added, `1/2` a `QQ`; the type takes them only through a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`, and refuses them otherwise, since coercions do not chain.
- The `=` pairs between a numeral type and a number type, eleven each way as built: deleted with the run-time numeral objects. "It was a wrong choice and it gets deleted." The probe tests `u = 0` for `u: NN32`, the one use the prototype saw: the checker fixes `0` at `NN32` from the other operand and folds it.
- Walk: no checker, so it meets the numeral at run time. At a fixed type it converts from the four numbers once, at the first evaluation of the place; at no type, the default; at a program's own type it instantiates the generic coercion with the numeral's four numbers as the static arguments, as walk fixes static parameters from run-time arguments (the preamble's own words, `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex:134-136`), runs the constructor call once for the place and keeps the result. Row 486 (walk refuses a `nat` static parameter used as a value) stands in the way. A refusal at a type with no coercion from the numeral type comes at run time under walk until walk runs the checker (P-12).
- A bare numeral with no type defaults, so the team's `NumberPrintTest:16` (a 32-digit numeral printed as written) prints 16 digits: his bend of 22:40, recorded. microGPT's untyped hyperparameters read as `RR64` the same way.
- "Static constraints" (the preamble, `:35-37`): the specification's "It is a static error" rules, checked before a program runs by the team's checkers beside the type checker (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`). His compile-time range check on a numeral coercion is one such constraint; under walk none exists until P-12.

- A static expression at a program's own type: repair 3's mix stands as the probe's default, the sign through the type's own `-`, every other static expression through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`; explained to him at 17:0x; confirmed at 17:2x UTC on 11-09: "I don't want anything change. I want that behavior with sign and what we [took as] repair three from last night." The complex test's notation is `3 + 4 i`, `i` a constant of the type, juxtaposition as multiplication (20:11, 20:13 on 11-08); batch 29's `imaginary` is not it.

The probe followed the snapshot in each case.

The snapshot's point 1 and section 4 give a numeral type no value at run time, and P-174 says a numeral type is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. == explorations/compile-ladder/plan-30/probes/draft-numerals.md:64-86

## 5. Step 4: the code generator, the runtime and the prelude

What was built:

- At a built-in target, batch 29's fold to a JVM constant is kept: the coercion desugarer retypes the numeral at the library type and the code generator emits the constant (`CoercionDesugarer.foldsTo`; `CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr`, `forFloatLiteralExpr`). The checker now finds that coercion through the library's generic coercion, so the type check of the conversion is the common mechanism; the fold itself is recognised by the target type, not by evaluating the coercion's body (decision 3). A negated radix-point numeral is negated after its one rounding, so `-0.0` is IEEE's negative zero.
- At a program's own type, the coercion generic over the four numbers is inlined at its site: the code generator takes the lifted coercion's body from the component, replaces each of the four numbers read as a value by its constant, a `ZZ`, and each static parameter of the coercion's type by the site's static argument, and compiles the body in the component class's static initializer into a `static final` field that the site reads (`CodeGen.inlinedNumeralCoercion`, `numeralCoercionDecl`, `emitNumeralCoercionSites`). No class is made per numeral, and the class loader stamps nothing for `v`, so `RTTIsize.of`'s `int` does not stand in the way of a 20-digit `v`. Why inlining and not one method that takes the four numbers as values: the body is already typed with the four numbers as `ZZ` values, so substituting constants needs no new method, signature or call; and a coercion of a generic type, `Gen[\T\]`, takes its type argument by the same substitution (`StaticTypeReplacer`, keeping the callee references' own generic schemas). Its limit: the coercion must be declared in the same component (section 10).
- A site at a program's generic type is now hoisted too, where its type names no type variable: `site(): Gen[\RR64\] = 3` gives one object per place (row 957's case; `numeralCoercionSiteDesc`).
- `-3` at a program's type compiles as the type's `-` on the hoisted coercion; the minus itself runs at each evaluation (section 10).
- The prelude (P-37's exception for the numerals, his words at 17:1x UTC on 11-09): the same five traits, `Numeral extends Number` with an `excludes` list of the prelude's number types, since they have no `comprises` clauses; the coercions of `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR64` and `RR32` in the generic form, their bodies through the prelude's own helpers (`bigOverflowingToLong`, `numeralToDouble`, `numeralToFloat`). `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are gone, with the `simpleIntLiteralArith` import. The prelude's own code wrote getters on numerals, `(1).asZZ` and `(1).asNN32` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:561-570`, `:814`, `:816`, `:750`, `:752`); they are respelled with the prelude's helpers or a typed binding.
- The runtime: a size read as a value no longer goes through an `IntLiteral`. The class loader stamps it as a `ZZ32`, `FZZ32.make`, or for a size beyond `ZZ32` `FZZ32.makeSize`, which raises the error of row 962 as before (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java`, `natMethod`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java`), and the code generator reads it without `asZZ32` (`CodeGen.forVarRef`). A numeral that no place typed compiles as its default constant, not as an `IntLiteral` (`forIntLiteralExpr`). `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java` loses its two literal branches.

Batch 29's hoisted sites fail the same way on the base (probe below). Not fixed; the test binds its operands first; filed as row 971.

The probe for row 971, on the base's code: a program `object Cell(s: String)` with `coerce(x: IntLiteral) = Cell(part(1) || part(2))` and `made(): Cell = 3`, compiled and run with `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base30 <tmp>/old-caches compile|run`:

## 6. Step 5: walk

What was built (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`, `Coercions.java`):

- A numeral still evaluates to its default, carrying its site and four numbers (batch 29's `Site`, read now through `NumeralNumbers`). At a place that fixes a type, walk finds that type's coercion generic over the numeral's kind of numeral type, checks its `where` clause at the four numbers, and runs its body once for the site and the type, with the four numbers bound as `ZZ` values and the coercion type's own static parameters bound to the target's; the parameter is bound to `()`, since no numeral value exists (`Numerals.numeralCoercion`, `convert`; `Coercions.numeralCoercions`). A folded static expression reaches a program's type through its default's type, as on the compiled path. `Numerals.object` and the numeral run-time type are gone (`numeralType` answers null), so no numeral object exists.

A second obstacle: an environment extended before it is blessed is refused, 'Internal error, attempt to copy environment still under construction' (`env/BetterEnv.java:110-114`); the two environments are blessed after their bindings. A third: walk keys a prefix operator as `prefix -` (`OprUtil.fixityDecorator`).

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskList
entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

# The static numerals, built: a prototype on both paths

The design is the curator's, the static numerals: section 3 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`, with sections 4 and 11. Batch 29 built another design, the field numerals: run-time value objects with the four numbers as fields and getters (`explorations/reviews/numeral-fidelity-2026-11-09.md`, section 2). This probe builds the static numerals in a worktree, on both paths, and measures what they cost. Nothing here weighs one design against the other.

- Base: `dd00743d9e`, `main`'s head when the probe started. Base build: `/home/user/fortress-base30`, built in place by `references/worktrees.md`. Worktree: `/home/user/fortress-proto-draft`, detached, seeded from it ("seeded from /home/user/fortress-base30 (dd00743d9e) in 3 s"). The worktree is removed at the end; its whole change is `draft-numerals.patch`, `git diff dd00743d9e` with the new files added by `git add -N`.
- Machine: `nproc` 4, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 2100 MHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; load at the first count 0.35, 0.57, 0.27 (`uptime`).
- Disk before the base build: `df -P /home/user` printed 20617500 1K-blocks available; after seeding, 20031136. A built tree is about 1.5 GB (`du -sh --exclude=.git /home/user/fortress`), so both trees left more than 14 G.
- Citations of the tree are at `dd00743d9e` unless they name the patch; the patch's code is cited by file and method, since the worktree is gone.

## 1. Where the snapshot and the record differ

The probe followed the snapshot in each case.

- P-173 says a place fixes a type when its declared type "is a numeral type". The snapshot's point 1 and section 4 give a numeral type no value at run time, and P-174 says a numeral type is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. Built: a binding at a numeral type is refused on both paths (`tests/NumeralTypeNoValueWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/LiteralTypeUnwritable.fss`).
- A static expression at a program's own type: the snapshot's section 11 says in one bullet "only through a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`" and in its last bullet "through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`"; P-174 says "through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`". Built: through the coercion from the folded value's default type, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, `QQ` for a quotient, `RR64` with a radix point.
- Row 486, which the brief and the snapshot's section 11 name as standing in walk's way, is `FIXED` (`53a6074ed`) and is about the compiled checker. Walk reads a `nat` used as a value already, as a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` from 2^31 (F-140). What stood in walk's way was elsewhere (section 6).
- The snapshot's section 2 quotes the Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` with three static parameters and `RadixPointNumeral[\n,m,10,v\]` with four; P-174 gives the four numbers to both. Built: the Draft's arities, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`; a coercion from a natural numeral reads `m` as 0 by not having it.

## 2. Step 1: the base build

- Commands, from `references/worktrees.md`: `git worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base30 dd00743d9e`, then in it `ant compileAll`, the library order and `bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, in the background with a log. Output: "BUILD SUCCESSFUL / Total time: 47 seconds / EXIT=0", and the five jars `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar`, `CompilerSystem.jar`; `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.
- `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base30 /home/user/fortress-proto-draft - dd00743d9e`.
- The base's checker, timed by `references/compiler.md`, "The checker's time": `time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out> <scratch>`, run from the base build: "#total 0 / #locations 0 / #crash none", "real 1m44.733s".
- The base's distance stage, `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out> <scratch>`, from the base build: "#total 0 / #crash none / #seconds 161 FortressLibrary 102".

## 3. Step 2: the one library

What was built (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `.fss`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `.fss`):

- The field numerals' two value objects, with their four getters, `asString`, `asFloat` and the 22 `=` pairs, are gone, with the two private helpers only `asString` used (`numeralDigits`, `numeralSuffix`). The `^` overloads on a numeral exponent (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`) are gone too: a numeral exponent converts at `^`'s other declarations.
- In their place, five traits with no members:

      trait Numeral extends Number end
      trait AnyNaturalNumeral extends Numeral excludes { AnyRadixPointNumeral } end
      trait AnyRadixPointNumeral extends Numeral end
      trait NaturalNumeral[\nat n, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyNaturalNumeral end
      trait RadixPointNumeral[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyRadixPointNumeral end

  The two `Any` traits exist only so that a type's coercion from each numeral type overloads with the other: two instantiations of different generic traits do not exclude each other otherwise. The library's own way for this is `AnyIntegral` above `Integral[\I\]`.
- Each of the eight number types takes a numeral by a coercion generic over the four numbers, whose body computes the value from them, as `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32` at `ZZ32`, `= Ratio(v, 1)` and `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = v / r^(m.asZZ32)` at `QQ`, and `= numeralRR64(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32)` at `RR64`, the library's one-rounding helper. `AnyIntegral`'s coercion chooses `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` from `v`.
- Lines: `git diff dd00743d9e --shortstat` over the four files: "4 files changed, 42 insertions(+), 145 deletions(-)".

Measured after this step, with the base's checker:

- Count stage: no total. "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=1)"; its output, `ClassCastException: class scala.runtime.BoxedUnit cannot be cast to class com.sun.fortress.nodes.IntExpr`, from `STypesUtil$outFinder` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:2151-2159`): the base checker types a numeral by the plain `NaturalNumeral`, cannot infer a generic coercion's sizes from it, leaves a size inference variable in the checked library, and the post-check walker returns `Unit` at an `IntExpr` position instead of reporting it. Row 291 holds the same crash from another trigger; its notes have 29 characters left, so this trigger is here only.
- Distance stage: "#total 8", one or two in each of six components, and six crash rows, each that `ClassCastException`.

## 4. Step 3: the checker

What was built:

- A numeral's type carries its four numbers as static arguments, `v` at any size: `3.125` is `RadixPointNumeral[\4,3,10,3125\]`, `3000000000` is `NaturalNumeral[\10,10,3000000000\]` (`impls/Misc.scala`, the literal cases; `compiler/Types.java`, `numeralType`). The four numbers come from one new helper that both paths and the code generator use, `nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java`, a port of batch 29's reading in `Numerals.java`. The analyzer compares sizes by their `BigInteger` values already (`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:120-131`), so `v` beyond 32 bits needed no change there. The kind check refused it: "Ill-formed static argument: 9223372036854775807", eight errors in five places; a numeral type's arguments and a numeral coercion's static arguments are now exempt (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`).
- Inference of a generic coercion's static arguments from the numeral's type is the checker's own static-argument inference (`CoercionOracle.checkCoercionTrait`, `inferStaticParams`); it worked unchanged. `getCoercionTargetsFrom`, which skipped every generic coercion, now admits one generic over a numeral's four numbers (`CoercionOracle.scala`), so a numeral still promotes a generic call (P-74).
- The range refusal as a static error: a coercion's `where` clause of size comparisons, as `where { v < 256 }`, is computed exactly at the inferred four numbers; a coercion whose clause fails is not a candidate, and the refusal reads "The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte." (`CoercionOracle.whereHolds`, `numeralRefusal`). Only comparisons of sizes are read; any other constraint is left to the checks that read it. At the eight library types the range refusal is batch 29's, by the value (`NumeralConversion.outOfRange`), not by a `where` clause (section 12, decision 6).
- Inside a coercion over a numeral type, the four numbers read as values are `ZZ`, exact integers; elsewhere a `nat` read as a value stays a `ZZ32` (P-173): `KindEnv.getType` and `markExact`, set from the declaration's parameter type in `impls/Decls.scala`.
- A numeral has no sign. The fold (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`) now marks its results by their text: prefix minus on a numeral as written keeps the written text after `-`, any other folded constant is written in parentheses, `(5)`. A radix-point numeral under a minus is folded the same way, its node holding the magnitude so that `-0.0` keeps its sign where it converts. At a library type the signed value converts directly, as before, so `-2147483648` at `ZZ32` folds exactly first. At a program's own type a negative constant is the type's own prefix minus on the coercion of the numeral as written: the checker checks that minus on a stand-in of the type and puts the coercion in its place (`STypeChecker.scala`, `coercions.negator`), with the component's own disambiguated prefix minus, which the fold now records per component (`prefixMinusOf`). A type without a prefix minus refuses it: "The numeral -3 at Plain needs a prefix minus on Plain, which it does not declare." Any other folded constant reaches a program's type only through its default's type (`CoercionOracle.buildCoercion`; `defaultFits` does the rest).
- P-173's default where nothing fixes a type is kept as it is. Two places changed because two numerals now have two types: an `if`, `case`, `try` or block whose results are numerals, alone or beside values that already fit, converts each numeral branch at the expected type in place (`numeralJoinInto`, `joinInto`, the `if`'s winning-clause path in `impls/Misc.scala`), and a tuple of numerals converts element by element in place (`buildCoercion`). Before, the checker coerced such a join or tuple as a whole, which ran a numeral's coercion at run time on an `IntLiteral` value; the static numerals have no value to run it on.
- Lines: `scala_src` and `compiler/Types.java`, "8 files changed, 316 insertions(+), 32 deletions(-)"; the fold and `NumeralNumbers.java`, "2 files changed, 161 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)".

Measured (count and distance stages over the one library, timed by `references/compiler.md`): the first run after the change, "#total 9 / #locations 5" (1m10.783s), the eight kind errors and one tuple join; then "#total 0 / #locations 0 / #crash none", "real 1m43.093s". The final runs are in section 8.

content.content:
## 9. What the whole design costs, by area

Lines are `git diff dd00743d9e --shortstat` over each area of the patch; rungs are my estimate in rungs of a batch, where batch 29 built the field numerals in rungs C, N, F and T.

- The one library: 4 files, 42 insertions, 145 deletions. Half a rung; it is most of rung N's text again, smaller.
- The prelude, under P-37's exception: 2 files, 51 insertions, 130 deletions. Half a rung, with the runtime.
- The checker: 8 files, 316 insertions, 32 deletions; with the fold and `NumeralNumbers.java`, 2 files, 161 insertions, 6 deletions. Two rungs: the numeral types and the `where` clause, and the sign and the joins.
- The code generator: 1 file, 118 insertions, 40 deletions; the runtime: 3 files, 16 insertions, 22 deletions. One rung.
- Walk: 2 files, 218 insertions, 58 deletions. One rung.
- Tests: walk 15 files, 220 insertions, 47 deletions; compiled 45 files, 283 insertions, 91 deletions; library 4 files deleted, 155 lines; the fold's unit test 9 lines changed. One rung, most of it the thirteen respelled pins and the promotions.
- In all: 87 files, 1434 insertions, 735 deletions; about six rungs, one batch. What section 10 leaves would add about two rungs, and the specification's revision (Appendix I, `literals.tex`) a third.
- The checker's time is unchanged within noise: the count stage over the one library took 1m44.733s on the base and 1m43.621s and 1m40.981s on the change, and the distance stage 161 s, and 159 s and 163 s (section 8).
- The library types' speed: at a built-in target the code is batch 29's fold to a JVM constant, unchanged; walk runs the library's coercion body once per place and type, cached by the site. No speed was measured (walk's timing is not taken, `references/interpreter.md`).

- Rows the prototype repairs but cannot close, since it lands nothing: 318, 362, 957 (first case), 961, 968, 969, 970, and row 513 for a numeral coercion.

## 11. Findings the record does not hold

- Row 971 (filed): on the compiled path a numeral site's coercion that spawns a task fails the load of the component's class, since the static initializer runs before the task pool; batch 29's sites fail so on the base (the probe in section 5).
- Row 972 (filed): a library component with a generic overloaded top-level function stores its inference cache tables into a class named without its package, and every compiled program dies at its static initializer. No library component has one today.
- Row 291's crash, `BoxedUnit cannot be cast` in the post-check walker, has a second trigger: a size inference variable left in a checked library (section 3). Not filed: the row's notes have 29 characters left; the trigger needs the probe's library to show.
- Walk's sizes are `long` (`IntNat.java`), and walk refuses a size above `NN32` when it binds one (`EvalType.java:252-262`); the record holds the second (F-140), not the first as the limit of a numeral's `v`.
- The checker coerces an `if`'s non-winning clauses, and a tuple of numerals at a tuple type, as whole expressions (`impls/Misc.scala:556-564`, `CoercionOracle.checkCoercionTuple`), so with batch 29's `IntLiteral` a numeral there was coerced at run time. Not a defect today; it matters only once numerals have no run-time value.
- The prelude's own code writes getters on numerals, `(1).asZZ` and `(1).asNN32` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:561-570`, `:750`, `:752`, `:814`, `:816`).

## 12. Decisions

1. The hierarchy, where the Draft is silent ("We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy", `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:93-95`, kept in the revived `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:123-126`): `Numeral` below `Number`, the record's "a sibling of the number types under `Number`" (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"); `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` at the Draft's arities, below two `Any` traits that exclude each other. Not taken: the Draft's `NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix` and `RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix` (the radix is `r`, as P-174 has it), its `Literal[\v\]`, and a generic `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` above both, which the exclusion rule forbids beside the two generic traits; `Numeral excludes { Number }`, which the promotion of P-74 cannot use: with it the team's `compiler_tests/InferO2Num` failed, one of the four failures of section 7's run of 45 tests. This is a decision not taken for the curator too (question 4).
2. The four numbers read as values inside a numeral coercion are `ZZ`; elsewhere a `nat` stays a `ZZ32` (P-173). The brief's "exact integers"; the alternative, every `nat` value a `ZZ`, changes P-173 and its tests.
3. At a built-in target the compiled fold is batch 29's, recognised by the target type; the checker reaches it through the library's generic coercion. The alternative, evaluating the library coercion's body at compile time, needs an evaluator in the compiler. Under walk the library's coercion body runs, as for any type.
4. On the compiled path the coercion is inlined at its site, not compiled as one method that takes the four numbers as values (section 5 gives why).
5. The fold marks its results by their text, `-3` and `(5)`, so that the checker, the code generator and walk tell a numeral as written from a negated one and from a folded static expression. The alternative, a field on the node, changes `Fortress.ast`.
6. At the library's eight types the range refusal stays batch 29's, by the value, not a `where` clause on each library coercion: `-2147483648` at `ZZ32` is a negative constant, which a `where` over `v` cannot see.
7. Under walk the parameter of a numeral coercion is bound to `()`, and the conversion runs when dispatch first asks whether a declaration admits the numeral.
8. The prelude keeps no `IntLiteral`; a size read as a value reaches the code as a `ZZ32`, with row 962's error kept.
9. The eight walk assertions of `u = 0` and its kin move to an `XXX` test that asserts the snapshot's answer, since the snapshot's section 11 states it; the compiled path's test keeps `u = 0`.

## 13. Questions for the curator, as decisions not taken

1. `u = 0` for `u: NN32`, under walk, and on the compiled path after the switch-over.
   - The question: with the `=` pairs over the numeral types deleted, `u = 0` meets two declarations: the library's `=` over `Any`, which the numeral's default `ZZ32` fits as it is, and `NN32`'s own `=`, which the numeral reaches by its conversion. Which runs?
   - Sources: the snapshot's section 11 (confirmed 11-09, 15:xx to 16:3x UTC): "the checker fixes `0` at `NN32` from the other operand and folds it"; the tree's rule "A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"), which walk applies (`OverloadedFunction.bestMatchForNumeralsInternal`); P-173's `gg(5, w)` (P-49).
   - Solutions: (a) a numeral reaches a declaration by its conversion before one it fits only at its default, where that declaration is more specific; this changes the tree's rule, and walk's dispatch; (b) `u = 0` is `false`, strict equivalence of an `NN32` and a `ZZ32`; (c) the `=` pairs stay, against "It was a wrong choice and it gets deleted".
   - Current behaviour: in the tree today the `=` pairs give `true`; with the prototype walk gives `false` and the compiled path `true`, since the prelude has no `=` over `Any`. Built: the compiled answer; walk's is the `XXX` test.
2. The library's own types and "a separate way in the compiler for the shipped numerics".
   - The question: the library's eight types take a numeral by the same generic coercion, and the checker finds it so; but the compiled fold to a JVM constant is recognised by the target type, and the range refusal is by the value, not a `where` clause. Is that the hole his words name, or the folding of a constructor call whose result is a JVM `int`?
   - Sources: the snapshot's section 11, first bullet; decisions 3 and 6.
   - Solutions: (a) keep it; (b) `where` clauses on the library coercions, with a reading of a negative constant's sign (`-2147483648` at `ZZ32` must fit); (c) a compile-time evaluator of the library coercions' bodies.
   - Current behaviour: (a), as batch 29 built it.
3. A folded static expression at a program's own type.
   - The question: through which coercion does `10/20`, or `2 + 3`, reach a program's type?
   - Sources: the snapshot's section 11, one bullet "only through a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`" and its last "through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`" (both 11-09, 15:xx to 16:3x UTC); P-174, "through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`" (section 1).
   - Solutions: (a) from the folded value's default type, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, `QQ` for a quotient, `RR64` with a radix point; (b) from `ZZ` for an integer, whatever its value, and `QQ` for the rest; (c) from `ZZ32` or `QQ` only.
   - Current behaviour: in the tree today the fold writes a constant as a numeral (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.written`), so it reaches a program's type through the type's coercion from the numeral type, as a numeral does; built: (a).
4. The numeral type hierarchy.
   - The question: which traits are the numeral types, and may a program extend them?
   - Sources: the Draft's note "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:93-95`, 2009); its `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]`, `NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix` and `Literal[\v\]` (`:83-129`); P-174, the four numbers.
   - Solutions: (a) the probe's five traits (decision 1); (b) the Draft's six types, which the rule that no type extends two instantiations of one generic trait refuses for `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` above both kinds; (c) (a) with `comprises` clauses, so that no program extends them, not tried.
   - Current behaviour: the tree's field numerals have three traits without static parameters; built: (a).
5. A coercion that spawns, at a place on the compiled path (row 971).
   - The question: where does a site's coercion run, given that a component's static initializer runs before the task pool?
   - Sources: P-176, "into a `static final` field filled when the class loads"; `MainWrapper.java:61-63`.
   - Solutions: (a) start the task pool before the program's classes load; (b) fill each site at its first use, on the task that reaches it, which changes P-176's "filled when the class loads"; (c) run the static initializer's coercions on the pool.
   - Current behaviour: the class's load fails, on the base and with the prototype; nothing was changed.
6. A coercion declared in another component than the numeral's site, on the compiled path.
   - The question: how does the compiled path apply a generic coercion whose body it cannot inline?
   - Sources: P-176; the snapshot's section 9, question 3, "What does `v` of a 20-digit numeral need in the checker, and in the class loader's stamped constants (F-129)?"; `RTTIsize.of`, which holds a size as an `int` (section 10).
   - Solutions: (a) one method per coercion that takes the four numbers as `ZZ` values, called once per place; (b) the class loader's instantiation, one class per numeral, with `RTTIsize` widened to a `BigInteger`; (c) inlining across components from the analyzed cache.
   - Current behaviour: the call stays at its site and is instantiated by the class loader; no test reaches it.

## 14. Where the Draft is silent, and what was chosen

- The hierarchy (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:123-126`, the team's note): decision 1.
- When a coercion runs: the Draft says nothing (the snapshot's section 2); P-176: once per place, at load on the compiled path, at the first evaluation under walk.
- The four numbers of a numeral with trailing zeros: as written, `3.14150` is 314150 and 5, batch 29's reading kept (`NumeralNumbers.of`).
- A radix indicator: the Draft's `...WithExplicitRadix` types are not built; `r` carries the radix, as P-174 has it.
- The sign: the Draft's natural numeral has no sign; the curator's 23:10 on 11-08 and repair 3 give the rest (P-174).

## 15. Commands worked out

- To see a compiled refusal of the base's code on a scratch program: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base30 <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `run P`.
- To respell compile-error pins that named `IntLiteral`: a script compiled each test's component, matched each pinned message line to the new one by its location, checked that the two are equal once `NaturalNumeral[\...\]` and `OR(...)` of them read back as `IntLiteral`, and wrote the new text with each backslash doubled for the property file. It is scratch, not committed; `XXX6at` and `XXX9q`, whose messages differ in more than the name, were rebuilt by hand from the new output.

## 16. For FACTS

None. The two defects are ledger rows 971 and 972; the prototype's measurements are of uncommitted code.

## 17. Defects

- Row 971: a numeral site's coercion that spawns a task fails the load of the component's class on the compiled path; on the base too (section 5).
- Row 972: a library component's generic overloaded top-level function stores its inference cache tables into a class named without its package (section 5); fixed in the patch, so the row stays open until a change lands.
- Row 291's crash has a second trigger (section 11); not filed, for the row's length.
- The prototype's own defects, each fixed in the patch before the gate's last round: a numeral in a join or a tuple coerced as a whole at run time (section 4), and the same in a `try`'s `catch` clause, which the gate's second round found (`NumeralDivByZeroCompiled`, section 8).

## 18. Sentences of the specification made false

The patch makes these false; they state the field numerals, which batch 29 built (F-345, row 969):

- `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:109-113`: "\Library\ declare these numbers as the getters \VAR{digits}, \VAR{fractionDigits}, \VAR{radix} and \VAR{digitValue} of \TYP{Numeral} ... They are fields of the numeral's value, not static parameters of its type: the three numeral types have no static parameters."
- `literals.tex:179-181`: "A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares a coercion from the numeral's type, ... or is a numeral type itself." The patch refuses a binding at a numeral type (section 1).
- `literals.tex:227-229`: "Inside the body of a coercion, two values of a numeral type are equal, and strictly equivalent, when their values $v/r^m$ are equal". With the static numerals a coercion's parameter has no value; the body reads the four numbers.
- `literals.tex:139-152`, the `\revision` box: "The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that the four numbers are fields of the numeral's value".
- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5005-5012`, the Change of `revival-numerals`: "its value holds the four numbers ... as the getters \VAR{digits}, \VAR{fractionDigits}, \VAR{radix} and \VAR{digitValue}"; and `:5013-5014`: "\secref{types-libraries} names \TYP{Numeral}, without static arguments".

## 19. Points to report

- The hierarchy, as a decision not taken: decision 1 and question 4.
- The method-or-inline choice: inline (decision 4, section 5).
- Row 486: not fixed, since it is `FIXED` and about the checker; walk's way around its real obstacle, the `long` sizes, is to bind the four numbers as values (sections 1 and 6).
- Where the snapshot and the entries differ: section 1.
- Where the Draft is silent: section 14.
- Each flip by name and line, with the team tests that change: section 8.
- The tests of the brief's list that could not be built on the compiled path (the interval, the `QQ` cases): section 7.

## Summary

The static numerals were built on both paths in a worktree of `dd00743d9e`; the uncommitted change is `draft-numerals.patch`, 87 files, 1434 insertions, 735 deletions.

- The one library: `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` under `Numeral`, and a coercion generic over the four numbers on each of the eight number types. The field numerals, their getters and the `=` pairs are gone. The hierarchy is a decision not taken.
- The checker: a numeral's type carries its four numbers, `v` at any size; the checker's own inference finds the coercion's static arguments; a `where` clause over them is computed exactly and refuses as a static error; P-173's default stands. Joins and tuples of numerals convert in place.
- The code generator and the runtime: a built-in target keeps batch 29's fold to a JVM constant, `-3` and `-2147483648` folded first. At a program's type the generic coercion is inlined once per place into a `static final`, `v` a `ZZ` constant, with no class per numeral and the type's `-` for negatives. The prelude carries the same declarations; `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are gone.
- Walk: each place converts at its first evaluation, from the four numbers bound as values; `-3` goes through the type's own `prefix -`; `Numerals.object` is gone. Row 486 did not stand in the way. Walk's `long` sizes did, and binding the four numbers as values goes around them.
- On the final code: count 0 (1m40.981s, base 1m44.733s); distance 0 (163 s, base 161 s); `ant testFast` passing (1515, 82 and 263 tests). The walk suite passed, 819 tests, and microGPT's quick checks 7 of 7 each, both before the last fix, which only the compiled checker runs.
- Cost: about six rungs (section 9); section 10's gaps and the specification add about three.
- Not built: a coercion declared in another component, on the compiled path; a site whose type names a type variable; the minus hoisted with the coercion. Under walk, `u = 0` gives `false` and refusals come at run time.
- Filed: rows 971 (a spawning coercion fails its class's load) and 972 (cache tables in a class without its package).
- Six questions for the curator (section 13): `u = 0`; the library's types and the fold by target type; a static expression's path; the hierarchy; a spawning coercion; a coercion from another component.

(* A numeral at a program's own reference type is one object for its site: the program's coercion from the numeral type runs once for each site, when the component's class loads, and each evaluation of the site reads its result. *)
component NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled
export Executable

object Cell(v: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = do
    println("coerce")
    Cell(bigToZZ64(v).asZZ32)
  end
end

sEq(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")

three(): Cell = 3
four(): Cell = 4

run(): () = do
  println("start")
  a = three()
  b = three()
  c = four()
  assert(sEq(a, b), "two evaluations of one site are one object")
  assert(NOT sEq(a, c), "two sites are two objects")
  assert(a.v, 3, "the first site's value")
  assert(c.v, 4, "the second site's value")
  println("PASS")
end


bigToZZ64(z: ZZ): ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong")
